## Why a joint smoother?

The syntax

```r
f(x1, x2, x3, x4)
```

defines one joint tensor-product GeDS spline. It is different from the additive
model

```r
f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4)
```

because the joint smoother can represent interactions among the covariates.
This vignette uses joint smoothers with `NGeDS`, `GGeDS`, and `NGeDSboost`,
and compares them with additive `NGeDSgam` and `NGeDSboost` models.
Joint smoothers use the SR stopping rule by default; the additive
one-dimensional `NGeDS` learners use RD. `GGeDS` uses SR by default.

```{r}
library("GeDS")

wiggly4 <- function(x1, x2, x3, x4) {
  2 * sin(pi * x1) * sin(pi * x2) *
    sin(pi * x3) * sin(pi * x4) *
    (1 + 0.15 * sin(4 * pi * x1) * sin(4 * pi * x2))
}

simulate_gaussian <- function(n, noise = 0.15) {
  data <- data.frame(
    x1 = runif(n), x2 = runif(n),
    x3 = runif(n), x4 = runif(n)
  )
  data$truth <- with(data, wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4))
  data$y <- data$truth + rnorm(n, sd = noise)
  data
}
```

## A four-dimensional Normal example

We fit the joint tensor with the direct Normal fitter and with boosting, then
compare these fits with additive local-scoring and boosting models. The joint
boost starts from the family's constant offset (`initial_learner = FALSE`).

```{r fit-normal, results='hide'}
set.seed(123)
train <- simulate_gaussian(1000)

fit_ngeds <- NGeDS(
  y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train
)

fit_boost_joint <- NGeDSboost(
  y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train,
  initial_learner = FALSE
)

fit_gam <- NGeDSgam(
  y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train
)

fit_boost_additive <- NGeDSboost(
  y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train
)
```

The four-way interaction is not additive, but its central peak gives the
default knot-insertion rule a detectable improvement from its first knots.
The number of linear internal knots selected in each direction is:

```{r}
lengths(fit_ngeds$linear.intknots)
```

To isolate the contribution of knot insertion, the zero-knot multilinear
tensor can be fitted with all four-way products of the original coordinates.
The comparison below uses the *linear* GeDS fit (`n = 2`), so the two models
differ in their knots rather than their spline degree.

```{r}
no_knot_tensor <- lm(y ~ x1 * x2 * x3 * x4, data = train)
set.seed(321)
test <- simulate_gaussian(1000, noise = 0)

round(c(
  `No internal knots` = mean((test$truth - predict(no_knot_tensor, test))^2),
  `GeDS-selected knots` = mean((test$truth - predict(fit_ngeds, test, n = 2))^2)
), 3)
```

The response depends on products of the coordinates: an additive model cannot
represent it exactly. For the surface slices, `x3` and `x4` are fixed at 0.25
while `x1` and `x2` vary over a grid.

```{r four-dimensional-surface, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2}
grid_values <- seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 45)
surface_data <- expand.grid(
  x1 = grid_values, x2 = grid_values,
  x3 = 0.25, x4 = 0.25
)

truth_surface <- with(
  surface_data,
  matrix(wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4), nrow = length(grid_values))
)
fitted_surface <- matrix(
  predict(fit_ngeds, surface_data, n = 4),
  nrow = length(grid_values)
)

surface_colours <- hcl.colors(30, "Blue-Red 3")
old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
image(grid_values, grid_values, truth_surface,
      col = surface_colours, xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "True 4D surface slice")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, truth_surface, add = TRUE,
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
image(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_surface,
      col = surface_colours, xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "Cubic NGeDS slice")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_surface, add = TRUE,
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
par(old_par)
```

The next plot follows a path through the four-dimensional space: `x1` and `x2`
vary together, while `x3` and `x4` are fixed. This reveals the interaction as
a curve along the path.

```{r four-dimensional-curves, fig.height=8}
slice_data <- data.frame(
  x1 = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 250),
  x2 = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 250), x3 = 0.25, x4 = 0.25
)
slice_truth <- with(slice_data, wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4))
slice_fits <- cbind(
  Truth = slice_truth,
  `NGeDS joint` = predict(fit_ngeds, slice_data, n = 4),
  `NGeDSboost joint` = predict(fit_boost_joint, slice_data, n = 4),
  `NGeDSgam additive` = predict(fit_gam, slice_data, n = 4),
  `NGeDSboost additive` = predict(fit_boost_additive, slice_data, n = 4)
)

layout(matrix(1:2, ncol = 1), heights = c(5, 2))
old_par <- par(mar = c(4, 4, 3, 1))
matplot(
  slice_data$x1,
  slice_fits,
  type = "l", lty = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4), lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2, 2),
  col = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"),
  ylim = range(slice_fits, finite = TRUE),
  xlab = "x1", ylab = "Response",
  main = "Interaction path: x1 = x2, x3 = x4 = 0.25"
)
par(mar = c(0, 0, 0, 0))
plot.new()
legend(
  "center", ncol = 2, cex = 0.85,
  c("Truth", "NGeDS joint (degree 3)", "NGeDSboost joint (degree 3)",
    "NGeDSgam additive (degree 3)", "NGeDSboost additive (degree 3)"),
  lty = c(1, 1, 2, 3, 4), lwd = c(3, 2, 2, 2, 2),
  col = c("grey20", "#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"),
  bty = "n"
)
par(old_par)
layout(1)
```

The y-axis includes every fitted curve on the original response scale.

## Repeated test-sample comparison

A single train/test split can be misleading. We repeat the experiment four
times and compare test mean squared errors against the known generating
function. Each box contains results from the same four simulated datasets.
The additive models cannot represent the four-way interaction exactly.

```{r gaussian-boxplots, fig.width=9, fig.height=6, results='hide'}
set.seed(123)
n_repetitions <- 4
normal_results <- vector("list", n_repetitions)

for (b in seq_len(n_repetitions)) {
  train_b <- simulate_gaussian(1000)
  test_b <- simulate_gaussian(1000, noise = 0)

  ngeds_b <- NGeDS(
    y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train_b
  )
  boost_joint_b <- NGeDSboost(
    y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4), data = train_b,
    initial_learner = FALSE
  )
  gam_b <- NGeDSgam(
    y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train_b
  )
  boost_additive_b <- NGeDSboost(
    y ~ f(x1) + f(x2) + f(x3) + f(x4), data = train_b
  )

  normal_results[[b]] <- c(
    "NGeDS joint (degree 3)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(ngeds_b, test_b, n = 4))^2),
    "NGeDSboost joint (degree 3)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(boost_joint_b, test_b, n = 4))^2),
    "NGeDSgam additive (degree 3)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(gam_b, test_b, n = 4))^2),
    "NGeDSboost additive (degree 3)" = mean((test_b$truth - predict(boost_additive_b, test_b, n = 4))^2)
  )
}

normal_mse <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, normal_results))
old_par <- par(mar = c(10, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(
  normal_mse, names = rep("", 4), xaxt = "n", log = "y",
  col = c("#0072B2", "#009E73", "#E69F00", "#D55E00"),
  ylab = "Test MSE (log scale)", cex.axis = 0.85,
  main = "Four-dimensional Gaussian experiment"
)
stripchart(normal_mse, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("grey15", 0.65), add = TRUE)
mtext(c("NGeDS joint\ndegree 3", "Boost joint\ndegree 3",
        "GAM additive\ndegree 3", "Boost additive\ndegree 3"),
      side = 1, at = 1:4, line = 3.5, cex = 0.75)
par(old_par)

round(vapply(normal_mse, median, numeric(1)), 3)
```

The additive models can capture marginal patterns, but not the four-way
interaction itself. The test MSE comparison therefore shows what the joint
tensor adds beyond separate univariate smoothers.

The joint boosting fit uses `initial_learner = FALSE` as specified above. The
common boxplot uses a log scale so that all four test-error distributions can
be compared on the same axes.

## A four-dimensional generalized-response example

The same tensor syntax is available in `GGeDS`. We generate Poisson counts with
a log-mean driven by the wiggly four-dimensional function. The higher count
level makes the shape visible above Poisson noise. For clarity and speed, this
example uses the linear Stage A tensor fit.

```{r poisson-fit, results='hide'}
simulate_poisson <- function(n) {
  data <- simulate_gaussian(n, noise = 0)
  data$eta <- 4 + 0.70 * data$truth
  data$mu <- exp(data$eta)
  data$count <- rpois(n, data$mu)
  data
}

set.seed(123)
poisson_train <- simulate_poisson(1000)

fit_ggeds <- GGeDS(
  count ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4),
  family = poisson(), data = poisson_train
)
```

The response-scale fitted surface can again be displayed as a two-dimensional
slice.

```{r poisson-surface, fig.width=9, fig.height=4.2}
poisson_surface_data <- surface_data
true_mean_surface <- with(
  poisson_surface_data,
  matrix(exp(4 + 0.70 * wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4)),
         nrow = length(grid_values))
)
fitted_mean_surface <- matrix(
  predict(fit_ggeds, poisson_surface_data, n = 2),
  nrow = length(grid_values)
)

old_par <- par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2.5, 1))
image(grid_values, grid_values, true_mean_surface,
      col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd"), xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "True Poisson mean")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, true_mean_surface, add = TRUE,
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
image(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_mean_surface,
      col = hcl.colors(30, "YlOrRd"), xlab = "x1", ylab = "x2",
      main = "GGeDS fitted mean")
contour(grid_values, grid_values, fitted_mean_surface, add = TRUE,
        drawlabels = FALSE, col = "grey25")
par(old_par)
```

For a small repeated comparison, we use an ordinary Poisson GLM with linear main
effects as a familiar benchmark. Thus, `count ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4` is compared
with the flexible joint tensor `count ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4)`. The loss is the mean
Poisson deviance relative to the true conditional mean.

```{r poisson-boxplots, fig.height=4.5, results='hide'}
set.seed(123)
poisson_results <- vector("list", n_repetitions)

for (b in seq_len(n_repetitions)) {
  train_b <- simulate_poisson(1000)
  test_b <- simulate_poisson(1000)

  ggeds_b <- GGeDS(
    count ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4),
    family = poisson(), data = train_b
  )
  fitted_mean <- predict(ggeds_b, test_b, n = 2)
  glm_b <- glm(
    count ~ x1 + x2 + x3 + x4,
    family = poisson(), data = train_b
  )
  glm_mean <- predict(glm_b, test_b, type = "response")

  poisson_results[[b]] <- c(
    "Linear Poisson GLM" = mean(poisson()$dev.resids(test_b$mu, glm_mean, 1)),
    "GGeDS joint tensor (degree 1)" = mean(poisson()$dev.resids(test_b$mu, fitted_mean, 1))
  )
}

poisson_deviance <- as.data.frame(do.call(rbind, poisson_results))
old_par <- par(mar = c(7, 4, 3, 1))
boxplot(
  poisson_deviance,
  names = c("Linear\nPoisson GLM", "GGeDS joint\ndegree 1"),
  col = c("grey75", "#CC79A7"),
  ylab = "Mean Poisson deviance", cex.axis = 0.85,
  main = "Four-dimensional Poisson experiment"
)
stripchart(poisson_deviance, vertical = TRUE, method = "jitter",
           pch = 19, col = adjustcolor("grey15", 0.65), add = TRUE)
par(old_par)

round(vapply(poisson_deviance, median, numeric(1)), 3)
```

Here the joint `GGeDS` tensor is compared with a model that uses all four
covariates, but restricts each of their effects to be linear.

## Moving to five dimensions

Nothing in the formula changes when a fifth coordinate is added. The following
example augments the earlier function with another oscillating interaction and
fits a five-dimensional tensor spline.

```{r five-dimensional-fit, results='hide'}
wiggly5 <- function(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5) {
  wiggly4(x1, x2, x3, x4) + 2 * sin(pi * x5) +
    0.6 * sin(2 * pi * (x5 + x1 * x3))
}

set.seed(123)
train5 <- data.frame(
  x1 = runif(1000), x2 = runif(1000), x3 = runif(1000),
  x4 = runif(1000), x5 = runif(1000)
)
train5$truth <- with(train5, wiggly5(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5))
train5$y <- train5$truth + rnorm(nrow(train5), sd = 0.20)

fit5 <- NGeDS(
  y ~ f(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5), data = train5
)
```

The default fit also selects linear internal knots in this five-dimensional
example:

```{r}
lengths(fit5$linear.intknots)
```

As before, a one-dimensional slice gives an immediate visual check of the fit.
The curves below are on their original response scale. Any vertical difference
is therefore a prediction error on this particular slice, not an adjustment
made to align the curves.

```{r five-dimensional-slice}
slice5 <- data.frame(
  x1 = 0.25, x2 = 0.40, x3 = 0.65, x4 = 0.30,
  x5 = seq(0.01, 0.99, length.out = 250)
)
truth5 <- with(slice5, wiggly5(x1, x2, x3, x4, x5))
prediction5 <- predict(fit5, slice5, n = 2)

plot(slice5$x5, truth5, type = "l", lwd = 3, col = "grey20",
     ylim = range(c(truth5, prediction5), finite = TRUE),
     xlab = "x5", ylab = "Response",
     main = "A slice through the five-dimensional tensor fit")
lines(slice5$x5, prediction5, lwd = 2, col = "#0072B2")
legend("topright", c("Truth", "NGeDS (degree 1)"),
       col = c("grey20", "#0072B2"), lwd = c(3, 2), bty = "n")
```

The fitted values match the mean training response, so an offset on this slice
does not indicate a missing intercept. A five-dimensional tensor is much harder
to estimate from 1,000 observations; this slice illustrates that limitation.

The same syntax extends to further dimensions, but tensor-product basis sizes
grow multiplicatively. In practice, higher-dimensional models should therefore
be accompanied by careful out-of-sample validation and by plots of informative
low-dimensional slices such as those above.
